subsection: 1. Structure of the Irish food industry

notes.h: How the food industry is organised
notes.b: The food industry takes raw produce from farms and fisheries, processes it into finished goods, and distributes and sells them through a service sector. It is organised in three levels, each depending on the one before it: a processor needs farmers' produce, and a retailer needs the processor's goods.
points: Primary sector: resource-based production, meaning farming, horticulture (growing fruit, vegetables and similar crops), fishing and fish farming (mariculture). It produces raw materials such as milk, cattle, sheep, pigs, poultry, eggs, grain, fruit, vegetables, fish and shellfish.

Secondary sector: manufacturing and processing, which converts raw materials into finished food and drink, such as milk into cheese, butter and milk powder, wheat into flour and bread, carcasses into cuts and meat products, or barley into beer and whiskey.

Tertiary sector: services that move, sell, support and regulate food, including transport, wholesale and retail, catering and food outlets, tourism and hospitality, research, education, advice, marketing and regulation.

Agri-food is one of Ireland's largest indigenous industries (industries that grew up in Ireland rather than being brought in from abroad), and most of its raw material is grown or reared on Irish farms.
The industry matters to the economy because it provides employment, much of it in rural areas, and earns income from export sales.
The UK and other EU member states are the main markets for Irish food overall, and much dairy and beef output is exported.
notes.tip: Primary, secondary and tertiary describe the production chain (farm, factory, service), which is different from product sectors such as dairy or meat. Tertiary is all services, not retail only: tourism, health, media and education count too. For a question on the three levels, give a definition of each with one or two examples.

notes.b: Besides the three levels, the industry is divided into product sectors. A single sector such as dairy can contain primary, secondary and tertiary activity, so keep the two lists apart.
points: Dairy and ingredients: milk, cheese, butter, yoghurt, cream and milk powder, plus dairy ingredients sold to other food manufacturers.
Meat and livestock: beef, lamb, pork and poultry, slaughtered and processed in licensed meat plants.
Beverages: beer and stout, whiskey and other spirits, fruit juice and bottled water.
Horticulture: fruit, vegetables and mushrooms, sold fresh or processed.
Seafood: fish and shellfish landed at Irish ports and processed for home and export sale.
Cereals and bakery: flour milling, bread, biscuits and breakfast cereals.
Prepared consumer foods: ready meals, snacks, confectionery and sauces sold in retail packaging.
notes.tip: The most common question asks you to name three sectors and give a product for each, so always pair every sector with one product. Naming any three with a product each earns the marks.

notes.b: Ireland produces far more of some foods than its small population can eat, so these are sold abroad. A climate and soil suited to grass means livestock and dairy output is much larger than home demand.
points: Dairy products, especially cheese, butter, milk powder and infant formula ingredients, are among Ireland's largest food exports.
Beef and lamb are exported to EU and non-EU markets.
Pork, poultry and processed meat products are also exported.
Irish whiskey, beer and stout are exported.
Seafood, including shellfish and farmed salmon, is exported from Irish ports.
Prepared foods and bakery products are sold to retailers and food service companies abroad.
notes.tip: When asked to name two major exports, say what the product is (for example cheese or beef), not just 'dairy'.

notes.b: Ireland imports foods it cannot grow, cannot grow all year round, or chooses to buy in for variety and price. Reasons include climate (tropical crops), seasonal gaps, consumer demand for variety and ethnic foods, ingredients for manufacturers and feed for livestock.
points: Tropical and out-of-season fruit, such as bananas, pineapples, oranges and avocados, which Ireland cannot grow commercially.
Coffee, tea and cocoa, which are grown in warmer countries.
Spices and sugar, which Ireland does not produce in quantity.
Soya and other animal feed ingredients used by Irish livestock producers.
Wine, and some processed foods such as chocolate and confectionery.
Rice, dried pasta, some vegetables and herbs, and sauces are also imported.
Ireland also imports some foods it exports, such as cheeses and meat products, for variety and price, so trade runs both ways.
Ireland is a net exporter of food overall, so the value of exports is greater than the value of imports.
notes.tip: Net exporter is about the total value of food traded, not that every food is exported: Ireland still imports many foods. If asked for two imports, tropical fruit, coffee, tea or wine all work.

notes.h: State agencies in the food industry
notes.b: Several State bodies support, develop and regulate the food industry. Each has its own job, so learn each name together with one function.
points: Bord Bia (the Irish Food Board) promotes Irish food, drink and horticulture at home and abroad, and develops national and international markets for Irish products.
Bord Bia runs quality assurance schemes for food producers, such as the Sustainable Beef and Lamb Assurance Scheme and the Sustainable Dairy Assurance Scheme, shown by a quality mark on pack.
Bord Bia's Origin Green programme records and verifies the sustainability commitments of food and drink companies: companies set measurable targets and their progress is independently verified.
Bord Bia helps Irish food companies with market research, buyer introductions and trade fairs.
Teagasc, the agriculture and food development authority, provides research, advice and training for farmers and food producers, so they can improve what they grow and make.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), the seafood development agency, develops the seafood sector and promotes seafood at home and abroad.
Enterprise Ireland supports export growth and innovation in Irish companies, including food and drink firms.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) sets and enforces food safety standards across the sector.
The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine is the government department responsible for the sector, covering policy and schemes.
notes.tip: Pair the agency name with one function in the same sentence. Two functions of Bord Bia that score: promote Irish food at home and abroad, support companies, develop markets, or run quality assurance schemes. Bord Bia promotes and certifies but is not the food safety body, which is the FSAI. Teagasc is for farming and food research and advice, while BIM is for seafood only.

notes.b: A local factory, business or home enterprise can be used to show how a food business fits into the industry structure. Work through the same set of questions for whichever business you choose.
points: Identify the business's sector, such as dairy, meat, beverages or bakery, and whether its main activity is primary, secondary or tertiary.
Record its raw materials, where they come from, and the finished products it makes.
Note its markets: local shops and customers, other Irish retailers, or export markets.
Assess its contribution to the area through jobs, local suppliers and the income it brings to rural communities, which is why the industry matters locally.
List the careers it offers, such as production operative, technologist, quality staff, chef or sales and marketing roles.

keyTerms.definition: The part of the food industry that produces raw materials from land and sea, such as farming, horticulture and fishing.
The part of the food industry that manufactures and processes raw materials into finished food products.
The services that distribute, sell, support and regulate food, including retail, catering, transport and advice.
A product or service sold to a buyer in another country.
A product or service bought from another country for use or sale in Ireland.
A country whose exports of a product or group of products are worth more than its imports of the same goods.
A certified programme that sets production standards for a food product and checks that producers meet them.

factCards.term: Three sectors of the Irish food industry, each with one product
factCards.definition: Dairy and ingredients: milk, cheese or yoghurt. Meat and livestock: beef, lamb or poultry. Beverages: beer, whiskey or juice.
Promote Irish food, drink and horticulture at home and abroad; support Irish food companies in marketing and exporting; develop national and international markets; run quality assurance schemes.
Dairy products such as cheese, butter and milk powder; beef and lamb.

factCards.term: Three types of food Ireland imports
factCards.definition: Tropical and out-of-season fruit; coffee, tea and cocoa; spices.

factCards.term: Three activities of the tertiary sector in food
factCards.definition: Distribution and transport; retail and food service; research, advice and regulation.

factCards.term: Two ways the food industry benefits the economy
factCards.definition: It creates employment, often in rural areas; it earns income from sales abroad.

factCards.term: Four state bodies that support the food industry
factCards.definition: Bord Bia, Teagasc, Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) and Enterprise Ireland.

questions.prompt: Outline three sectors of the Irish food industry, giving one food product produced in each sector.
questions.model: Dairy and ingredients: milk, cheese, butter or yoghurt. Meat and livestock: beef, lamb, pork or poultry. Beverages: beer, whiskey or juice. Accept seafood, horticulture or bakery, each with a relevant product. One mark for each sector named and one for each product linked to it.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the Irish food industry, identifying its primary, secondary and tertiary sectors. Discuss the major food exports and imports and the role of a state agency in supporting the industry.
questions.model: Primary sector: farming, horticulture and fishing produce raw materials such as milk, cattle, grain, fruit and fish. Secondary sector: manufacturing converts raw materials into finished goods such as cheese, meat products and bakery items. Tertiary sector: transport, wholesale and retail, catering, research and regulation. Structure by sector: dairy and ingredients, meat and livestock, beverages, horticulture, seafood, cereals and bakery, prepared consumer foods. Exports: dairy products, beef and lamb, pork and poultry, whiskey, beer and stout, seafood. Ireland is a net exporter, mainly to the UK and EU. Imports: tropical fruit, coffee, tea and cocoa, spices, sugar, animal feed ingredients, wine and processed foods that Ireland cannot produce economically. Agency role: Bord Bia promotes Irish food at home and abroad, develops markets, supports companies with marketing and runs quality assurance schemes; Teagasc, BIM and Enterprise Ireland support research, the seafood sector and exporting firms.
